▪️ Pace: “If we go steadily in smaller increments, more frequent, smaller rises, it’s easier for businesses and households to manage around that. It’s less disruptive to the overall economy than moving in sharper, more aggressive movements.”

▪️ On 50bp: “I don’t think we’re behind the curve today, but if we get behind the curve, then that might be something that we need to consider.” She’ll “certainly have an open mind walking into that December meeting.”

▪️ The nuance: She dissented for a hike in October, so she remains on the hawkish side looking for every-meeting increases. 

So of the six December voters who’ve spoken this week, including two of the hawks, only Waller has explicitly advocated for a larger hike in December. Key voice NY Fed President Williams speaks tonight.

US existing home sales (closings) fell 5.5% in October to a 3.75M annual rate, the lowest since August 2010 and well below the 3.85M expected. September was revised down to 3.97M (+1.0%, from +1.5%).

Sales were down 8.8% from a year ago, the third straight annual decline, and have been below 4M for three straight months.

▪️ Median price $416.7K, +0.4% y/y, the smallest gain since February but the 40th straight annual increase, now 5.9% below June’s $442.8K record. 
▪️ Inventory 1.59M, +4.6% y/y and the most for any October since 2019. Months’ supply at current sales rate 5.1, the highest since late 2015.
▪️ Regions: the West fell 9.7% to 650K, its slowest pace in data back to 1999. The South (−6.5% to 1.73M) and Midwest (−3.2% to 900K) both hit their lowest in more than a decade. The Northeast was flat at 470K.
▪️ Condo sales fell to 340K, the lowest in records back to 1999. Single-family sales fell 5.8% to 3.41M.
▪️ Sales fell from a year ago in every price tier, including $1M+ (−6.6%), which had been the only tier still growing in August and September.
▪️ NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7, the lowest (least affordable) since mid-2025, with the mortgage rate NAR uses at 7.41%.
▪️ First-time buyers 29% of sales (32% a year ago), investors and second-home buyers 20% (16%), and 35 median days on market.

October closings mostly reflect contracts signed in August and September at 6.67% to 6.86% mortgage rates. Freddie Mac’s 30-year averaged 7.33% in October, the highest since November 2023, and September pending sales hit a record low. 

That backs up Yun’s warning last month that Q4 closings could be “measurably down.” Supply at a decade high hasn’t broken prices yet, though Redfin says 36% of homes sold in October had at least one price cut, the most in its data.

Source: National Association of Realtors, Freddie Mac, Bloomberg, Redfin

Goldman: While the effects of cost pressures on energy-sensitive core components, such as airfares in the US and Canada, tend to materialize quickly, upstream price increases—which partially reflect the indirect price pressures of energy prices on upstream production—typically take 6-12 months to fully pass through to consumer prices (Exhibit 4, left). 

In addition, on average, each 1% increase in producer and import prices raises annualized core inflation by 0.1-0.2pp after 6-12 months (Exhibit 4, right). 

Applying the peak cumulative impulse to observed upstream price increases implies an average 0.8pp boost to core inflation relative to the pre-war baseline (although the import price contribution may be somewhat overstated, as higher prices for the types of semiconductors imported for use in data centers have little readthrough to consumer prices). These patterns suggest residual cost pressures will continue to boost inflation into the first half of 2027.

@C_Barraud's Wednesday Brief included a ZeroHedge article on Morgan Stanley's research into productivity which found that just 12 of 64 US industries, the ones most exposed to AI, now generate roughly 83% of US productivity growth. 

Last Thursday’s Q3 productivity report (+3.6% annualized vs. a 2.7% consensus, with unit labor costs down 0.7%) gave the AI-disinflation camp a victory lap. MS’s industry-level breakdown, which runs through Q2, shows as of then it was driven by a narrow base:

▪️ Output per employee rose 2.4% y/y, about twice the 20-year average pace, but 2.0pp came from the 12 high-AI industries, while the other 52 contributed just 0.4pp combined.
▪️ The concentration is rising, not fading: a year earlier the split was 1.4pp vs. 1.0pp, so the high-AI share has gone from about 58% to 83%.
▪️ High-AI output per employee is running about 7%-8% y/y, the mid-AI group is decelerating, and the low-AI group is contracting.
▪️ The leaders are the industries building, selling or trading the AI boom: data processing and internet publishing +27.0%, securities and investments +17.6%, and publishing (incl. software) and computer systems design about +9% each.
▪️ Where most Americans work, though, it’s a different story: hospitals +0.3%, construction flat, restaurants and bars +0.9%, food and beverage stores −4.7%, trucking −11.4%, and general merchandise stores −11.8%.
▪️ Even inside the high-AI group it’s mixed: computer manufacturing swung from +13.0% at the end of 2025 to −1.1% in Q2, and legal services, supposedly ground zero for AI disruption, fell 1.8%.
▪️ What’s new vs. six months ago: about half of the high-AI industries are now cutting jobs, although MS still sees faster output, not layoffs, as the main driver.

MS’s read is that the gains reflect capital deepening in AI-related industries rather than business-process changes across the broader economy. That lines up with the flat total factor productivity Apollo’s Torsten Slok and SocGen’s Albert Edwards have flagged, and with Goldman’s Census-based adoption data: only 24.6% of US establishments use AI regularly, though adoption is approaching 50% in information, professional services and finance.

This matters for the Fed more than for the productivity headline. The parts of the CPI basket driving the inflation problem, like groceries, trucking and medical care, sit in the low-AI industries where productivity is flat to falling, which is also where elevated supercore (+0.40% in October) readings are coming from. 

Those services pressures were flagged by several Fed members this week. And the gains aren’t reaching workers either: the labor share of nonfarm business output fell to 53.0% in Q3, the lowest since the series began in 1947.

Nvidia ($NVDA) is down nearly 8% after hours after the Wall Street Journal reported the board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang. Multiple outlets report directors are meeting today to decide his future. 

The stock is now down a third from its October 6 record close and at its lowest level since July 2025. Including tonight’s drop, Reuters puts Nvidia’s lost market value at about $600B since the board opened its investigation on Sunday.

Key points:

▪️ This went from a personal scandal to a governance problem in three days. On Sunday Huang admitted an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a Megaspeed executive US intelligence officials reportedly believe works for China’s Ministry of State Security. On Wednesday the New York Times reported a second relationship, with Kimberly Powell, who runs Nvidia’s healthcare business. 

▪️ Further, Bloomberg’s analysis of trade records shows Megaspeed imported over $4.6B of Nvidia products, much of it in a surge ahead of planned US licensing rules in May 2025. Bloomberg also found Megaspeed brought in 50,000 more chips than Nvidia’s audit located in its data centers. The Justice Department is now leading multiple investigations involving Alice Huang, and Commerce has been probing Megaspeed since late 2024.

▪️ There’s no succession plan. Huang has roughly 60 direct reports and has said he doesn’t believe in formal succession planning. Nvidia’s own proxy says it’s “highly dependent” on its longtime executive team. Bloomberg reports the board is working with an outside firm on candidates and weighing an interim CEO while it searches.

▪️ Washington upcoming. Huang is due before a closed-door session of House national security committees on November 18. His relationship with President Trump helped win approval for chip sales to China, and those decisions are now drawing scrutiny from lawmakers.

▪️ This reaches past Nvidia’s own stock. Huang is the AI trade’s chief salesman and dealmaker. Nvidia held about $63B in public stakes as of June 30, plus private bets on OpenAI and Anthropic, and a $500B financing pool with private-capital partners. A leadership change raises questions about those and future commitments and about Nvidia’s China strategy.

▪️ The selloff is spreading to the companies Nvidia has backed. All seven of Nvidia’s major public stakes are down at least 1% after hours. CoreWeave is -6.4%, Nebius -3.9%, Coherent -3.2%, Intel -2.5%, Nokia -1.9%, Synopsys -1.7% and SpaceX -1.2%. Oracle, tied in through OpenAI’s Stargate rather than an Nvidia stake, is -2.8%. Hyperscalers other than Oracle in contrast are little changed (Meta is the worst -0.8%) and competitors are up (AMD +3.2%).
